passages.happening:
The Philistines gather all their forces at Aphek, while Israel camps by the spring in Jezreel (verse 1). As the Philistine lords march out with their companies, David and his men march at the rear with Achish (verse 2).

The Philistine commanders ask, “What about these Hebrews?” Achish answers that this is David, once Saul's servant, who has been with him a long time, and he has found no fault in him (verse 3).

The commanders are angry. They tell Achish to send him back to the place he was given. ‘He must not go down with us into battle only to become our adversary during the war’ (verse 4). What better way for David to win back his master's favor than with the heads of their men? ‘Is this not the David about whom they sing in their dances’ (verse 5), the song of Saul's thousands and David's tens of thousands?
passages.hearers:
The last chapter left David trapped. He had agreed to march with the Philistines against Israel. If he fought, he would be killing his own people and fighting the anointed king he had twice refused to harm. If he refused or turned in the battle, his cover was gone and his men were in danger. This chapter frees him without David lifting a finger.

The narrator steps back in time to tell it. The Philistines are still gathering at Aphek, before they move to Shunem. Aphek, at the southern edge of the Sharon plain near the source of the Yarkon River, was a natural place to muster before marching north along the coast. The Philistines had gathered there before, on the day the ark was captured.

The Philistines were five city-states, each with its own ruler, and the chapter shows how that worked. Achish, David's patron, cannot overrule the other commanders. Their fear rests on experience. Earlier in Saul's reign, Hebrews who had served with the Philistines went over to Israel in the middle of a battle. Six hundred Hebrew fighters at the rear of their army was exactly the risk no commander would want.

Hebrews is the name foreigners often use for Israelites in the Old Testament. It marks David's men as outsiders whose loyalties lie elsewhere. And the old song follows David even here. It made Saul jealous. Now it makes the Philistines wary.

The word for adversary is satan, used here of a human enemy. Only later in the Old Testament does it become a title for a heavenly accuser.
passages.later: Chronicles remembers this day from the other side: ‘the Philistine rulers consulted and sent David away’ (1 Chronicles 12:19). The same word for adversary is used of a human enemy elsewhere: ‘Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite’ (1 Kings 11:14).
passages.asks: The Philistine commanders saw David more clearly than Achish did. Ask whether someone you dismissed as unfair might have seen what you could not. And ask whether God has ever got you out of a trap of your own making without your doing anything at all.

passages.happening:
Achish calls David. He swears by the LORD that David has been upright in his sight, and that he would gladly have him march with the army. But the lords do not approve of him. ‘Therefore turn back now and go in peace’ (verse 7).

“But what have I done?” David replied. “What have you found against your servant, from the day I came to you until today, to keep me from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” (verse 8).

Achish says that David is ‘as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God’ (verse 9), but the commanders will not have him in the battle. He is to leave at first light (verse 10).

So David and his men get up early and go back to the land of the Philistines. ‘And the Philistines went up to Jezreel’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is almost all talk, and it runs on irony. Achish praises David's loyalty three times, yet the reader knows from chapter 27 that David has been deceiving him all along. The commanders, whom Achish thinks unfair, are the only ones who read the situation rightly.

Achish swears by the LORD, using the name of Israel's God, perhaps out of courtesy to David. He compares David to an angel of God, a picture of perfect goodness and wisdom. The praise is sincere, and it is misplaced. Achish calls David upright ‘in my sight’, and those words matter: his judgment rests on what he has been allowed to see.

David's protest is a masterpiece of double meaning. He asks why he cannot fight ‘the enemies of my lord the king’. Achish hears himself as the lord the king. But Israel's king is Saul, and the words could just as well mean that David wants to fight the Philistines. The narrator never says what David meant.

The point is that God, working through the suspicion of Philistine commanders, gets David out of the trap. The chapter never says that God acted, but the outcome shows his hand. David will be miles away when Saul falls. No one will be able to say that the new king had a part in the old king's death.
passages.later:
Proverbs says what this chapter shows without saying it: “The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases” (Proverbs 21:1).

Others will later use Achish's words to praise David as king: ‘for my lord the king is able to discern good and evil, just like the angel of God’ (2 Samuel 14:17).
passages.asks: Achish trusted what he had been allowed to see. Ask whether you judge people only by what they show you. And ask where God may be keeping you out of a battle you should never have agreed to fight.
